metadata.title: Precision vs Recall: Why Accuracy Can Mislead You
metadata.factual_scope: Accessible classification-metric explainer using one explicitly hypothetical transaction example.
metadata.methodological_boundary: Accuracy remains useful; metric choice depends on class balance, decision context, and the real-world costs of false positives and false negatives.
metadata.production_gate: Direct clean-master production authorized after internal QC; no separate review/slate export.

beats.narration_text: Hi, my name is Ushasvi Rachel, and this video is about precision, recall, and why accuracy alone can be misleading in machine learning. A model can be highly accurate and still fail at the one thing we actually care about.

shot.visual_intent: Integrated presenter introduction and accuracy-versus-critical-failure hook.

beats.narration_text: Accuracy is the proportion of all predictions that are correct. It is a useful summary, but it may be incomplete when classes are imbalanced. A strong overall score can hide weak performance on a small but important positive class. That does not make accuracy useless; it means we need more context.

shot.visual_intent: Accuracy definition, value, and minority-class blind spot.

beats.narration_text: Consider a hypothetical example with one thousand transactions. Nine hundred ninety are normal, and ten are fraudulent. A model predicting normal every time gets nine hundred ninety cases correct, producing ninety-nine percent accuracy. But it detects zero fraud. The score is mathematically correct while missing the purpose of the model.

A confusion matrix separates four outcomes. A true positive correctly identifies a positive case. A false positive predicts positive when the case is negative. A false negative misses a true positive case. And a true negative correctly identifies a negative case.

shot.visual_intent: Large full-stage confusion matrix with all four correct definitions.

beats.narration_text: Precision asks: of everything the model predicted as positive, how many were actually positive? Conceptually, it is true positives divided by true positives plus false positives. Precision focuses on the reliability of positive predictions.

shot.visual_intent: Precision question, contributing outcomes, and conceptual formula.

beats.narration_text: Precision matters when false alarms are costly. In fraud detection, repeatedly flagging legitimate transactions may unnecessarily block users. Higher precision can reduce those false alarms. But high precision alone does not guarantee that the model finds enough actual fraud.

shot.visual_intent: False-positive cost pathway using a legitimate transaction.

beats.narration_text: Recall asks: of all actual positive cases, how many did the model successfully find? Conceptually, it is true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives. Recall focuses on coverage of the positive class.

shot.visual_intent: Recall question, contributing outcomes, and conceptual formula.

beats.narration_text: Recall matters when missing a positive case is costly. In fraud detection, a false negative means actual fraud was missed. Finding more positive cases may justify investigating some additional false alarms. But the acceptable balance depends on the real decision setting.

shot.visual_intent: False-negative cost pathway and contextual tradeoff.

beats.narration_text: Changing a classification threshold can often increase recall while reducing precision, or increase precision while reducing recall. This is not always a fixed one-for-one tradeoff. The outcome depends on the model, its scores, and the data distribution.

shot.visual_intent: Threshold slider and balanced precision-recall implications.

beats.narration_text: The best metric depends on context. Fraud systems may prioritize missed fraud. Spam filters must avoid hiding legitimate email. In medical screening, missing a true positive can have serious consequences, but real clinical decisions require far more than one model metric. No single metric is universally most important.

shot.visual_intent: Three-column fraud, spam, and careful medical-screening contexts.

beats.narration_text: F1 combines precision and recall using their harmonic mean. It can be useful when both metrics matter and a single summary is helpful. But F1 is not automatically superior to accuracy, and it is not automatically the best metric for every problem.

shot.visual_intent: F1 as a balanced summary with explicit limitation.

beats.narration_text: Model evaluation should reflect the real-world cost of mistakes. Define the positive class, examine false positives and false negatives, choose metrics that match the decision, and validate the threshold. Before choosing a score, ask: what kind of error matters most?

shot.visual_intent: Evaluation workflow and central error-cost question.

beats.narration_text: Accuracy tells you how often the model is right overall. Precision tells you how reliable its positive predictions are. Recall tells you how many actual positives it found. Accuracy tells you how often the model is right. Precision and recall tell you what kinds of mistakes it is making.

shot.visual_intent: Three-metric summary and exact closing takeaway.
